Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham.  Watch fans mark Hillsborough » . Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

(CNN) — More than 28,000 Liverpool supporters gathered at Anfield on Wednesday for a memorial marking two decades since the Hillsborough disaster. The occasion was especially moving for those assembled on the stadium’s Kop.

On April 15, 1989, 96 fans were killed before Liverpool’s FA Cup semifinal against Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday’s ground. It remains the deadliest disaster in English sporting history.

At 3:06 p.m. local time (1406 GMT), Liverpool paused in remembrance. Bells rang from the city’s two cathedrals and civic buildings to honor those who died. Ninety-six candles were illuminated on the Kop, while separate commemorations were held in Hillsborough and Nottingham.

Liverpool’s current players stood in solemn silence as hymns were performed and the names of all the victims were read aloud. Kenny Dalglish, the club legend who managed Liverpool when the tragedy occurred, followed with a brief prayer.

The emotional service was partly organized by Liverpool Mayor Steve Rotherham, who had attended the match 20 years earlier.

“Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK,” he said. “I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion.”

Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard also spoke during the week about the disaster. His cousin, 10-year-old Jon-Paul Gilhooley, was its youngest victim.

“Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget,” Gerrard said. “So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them.”

The fatal crush began shortly before kickoff after a gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened, with devastating results. Although the game initially got underway, it was quickly called off at 3:06 p.m. once the magnitude of the emergency became apparent.

Soon afterward, the British government appointed Lord Justice Taylor to lead an investigation whose findings would profoundly reshape football. Taylor strongly criticized the policing at Hillsborough. His most consequential proposals called for perimeter fences to be removed and stadiums to be converted into all-seater venues.

The Taylor report also absolved Liverpool supporters of responsibility. That finding followed sensational tabloid coverage blaming fans, which caused widespread outrage across Merseyside.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown addressed the dispute in an interview broadcast on Liverpool’s official television channel.

“It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day,” Brown said. “That’s probably what matters most — that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent.”

“Let’s never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other,” he added.

Nevertheless, anger and resentment remain in Liverpool over what many regard as the failure to secure justice for the dead. Those feelings were evident when Andy Burnham, the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, stepped forward to speak.

As Burnham addressed the gathering, the entire crowd stood and sang, “Justice for the 96.” The chant thundered around Anfield, making the depth of dissatisfaction over the absence of official accountability unmistakable to Burnham, an Everton supporter.

The service ended appropriately with Gerry Marsden leading the crowd in a rendition of Liverpool’s anthem, “You’ll Never Walk Alone.”

**LIVERPOOL, England (CNN) —** Thousands of people filled Liverpool’s Anfield stadium Wednesday to mark the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, one of the darkest days in British sporting history.

Families of the victims joined survivors, supporters and members of Liverpool Football Club for an emotional memorial service honoring the 96 men, women and children then recognized as having died following the April 15, 1989, tragedy.

The disaster occurred during an FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Hillsborough stadium in Sheffield, when overcrowding in standing terraces led to a fatal crush.

At 3:06 p.m. — the time the match was stopped — Liverpool fell silent for two minutes. Public transport paused, church bells rang and flags were lowered across the city.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benítez and players including captain Steven Gerrard and Jamie Carragher attended the service, alongside former players, officials and representatives from Everton, Liverpool’s city rival. Candles were lit and the names of the victims were read aloud.

The crowd also renewed its call for accountability. When government minister Andy Burnham addressed the service, chants of “Justice for the 96” echoed around the stadium, reflecting the families’ long-running campaign for the full circumstances of the disaster to be disclosed.

The 1989 Taylor Report concluded that the main cause was a failure of police control, but relatives continued to challenge the original inquest findings and the way authorities handled the disaster and its aftermath.

The ceremony ended with the singing of Liverpool’s anthem, **“You’ll Never Walk Alone,”** as supporters raised scarves across the Kop.

*Editor’s note: At the time of the 2009 memorial, the official death toll was 96. It was formally raised to 97 in 2021 after a coroner ruled that Andrew Devine died from injuries sustained at Hillsborough.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Liverpool Falls Silent as Hillsborough’s 20th Anniversary Renews Calls for Justice

**LIVERPOOL, April 15, 2009** — Liverpool paused in grief and solidarity on Wednesday as tens of thousands gathered at Anfield and people across the city marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, renewing demands for the full truth about the deaths of 96 football supporters.

At 3.06pm — the time the 1989 FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest was stopped — a two-minute silence was observed inside the stadium and across the city. Public buildings lowered their flags, businesses halted work, and transport services joined the tribute. Bells sounded at Liverpool’s cathedrals, while ferries on the River Mersey marked the moment with their horns.

Anfield, normally filled with the noise of football, became the focus of a solemn memorial service attended by about 30,000 supporters, bereaved relatives, former players, club officials and civic leaders. The names of the victims were read aloud, one by one, as 96 candles burned in their memory.

Scarves, flowers and handwritten messages covered the Hillsborough memorial outside the stadium. On the Kop, supporters held their scarves above their heads before singing Liverpool’s anthem, “You’ll Never Walk Alone,” turning the familiar football song into a declaration of remembrance and support for the families.

The service was led by the Bishop of Liverpool, the Right Reverend James Jones. Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard and vice-captain Jamie Carragher were among those taking part, alongside manager Rafael Benítez and former manager Kenny Dalglish, who led the club at the time of the disaster and attended many of the victims’ funerals.

The ceremony also became an unmistakable expression of anger over the long struggle for accountability. When Culture Secretary Andy Burnham addressed the crowd, supporters interrupted with chants of “Justice for the 96.” The chant was repeated around Anfield, underlining the widespread belief that the official response to the disaster had failed both those who died and those who survived.

Hillsborough occurred on April 15, 1989, when crushing developed in the Leppings Lane terraces at Sheffield Wednesday’s stadium during the FA Cup semi-final. Ninety-four people died that day; two more later died from their injuries. Hundreds were hurt, many of them physically or psychologically scarred for life.

The Taylor Inquiry later concluded that the main cause was a failure of police control. It rejected claims that drunken or ticketless Liverpool supporters had caused the disaster. Yet families have continued to challenge the 1991 inquest verdicts of accidental death and the decision to impose a 3.15pm cut-off for evidence, arguing that the restriction prevented proper examination of the emergency response after the crush began.

Campaigners have also demanded the disclosure of all government, police and emergency-service documents connected to the disaster. For many relatives, the anniversary was not only a day of mourning but another stage in a campaign that has lasted two decades.

Across Liverpool, the tributes extended well beyond Anfield. Flags flew at half-mast at civic buildings, and moments of silence were observed in workplaces, schools and public spaces. Everton supporters and officials joined the commemorations, reflecting a sense that Hillsborough’s loss belongs to the entire city, regardless of club allegiance.

Red and blue scarves appeared together among floral tributes, while shop windows displayed messages of remembrance. The unity echoed the response in 1989, when Everton fans stood alongside their Liverpool counterparts and the city’s football rivalry gave way to shared grief.

Inside Anfield, the atmosphere moved between silence, prayer and defiance. Relatives sat close to the pitch, many carrying photographs of those they had lost. The reading of the names emphasized the human scale of the tragedy: children, teenagers, parents, brothers, sisters and friends who had travelled to watch a football match and never returned home.

The youngest victim was 10-year-old Jon-Paul Gilhooley, a cousin of Gerrard. Many of those who died were in their teens and twenties.

For the families, the passage of 20 years has done little to lessen the pain or the determination to challenge what they regard as institutional failures and injustice. Their campaign has focused not only on the events that led to the crush but also on the treatment of supporters afterward, including allegations circulated in sections of the media that fans had behaved violently or obstructed rescuers.

Those claims have long been condemned in Liverpool and were contradicted by the findings of the Taylor Report. Survivors and witnesses have repeatedly described supporters trying to save one another, using advertising boards as makeshift stretchers and administering first aid while the emergency response struggled to cope.

As the service ended, the crowd again sang “You’ll Never Walk Alone.” The final notes carried around the stadium before giving way to the chant that has accompanied the families through years of hearings, reports and rejected appeals:

“Justice for the 96.”

Twenty years after Hillsborough, Liverpool’s message was clear: the dead would continue to be remembered, and the campaign for truth and accountability would not end.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the events at Anfield during the emotional memorial for the Hillsborough victims, while also explaining the disaster, the Taylor inquiry, and its impact on English football.
counterfactuals.output:
At Anfield, thousands gathered in solemn remembrance of the Liverpool supporters killed at Hillsborough. The victims’ names were read aloud, candles and floral tributes were displayed, and the crowd observed a silence at 3:06 p.m.—the time the 1989 FA Cup semi-final was stopped. The service included prayers, speeches, and an emotional rendition of “You’ll Never Walk Alone,” alongside renewed calls for truth, accountability, and justice for the families.

The disaster occurred on 15 April 1989 at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough stadium during Liverpool’s FA Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. Severe overcrowding developed in fenced standing pens at the Leppings Lane end after police opened an exit gate and failed to direct incoming supporters away from already packed central areas. The resulting crush ultimately caused 97 deaths and injured hundreds. Supporters were wrongly blamed for years; later investigations and the 2016 inquests concluded that the victims were unlawfully killed and that fan behavior did not cause the disaster.

Lord Justice Taylor’s inquiry identified failures of police control as the principal cause and exposed serious shortcomings in stadium design and safety management. Its recommendations transformed English football: top grounds became all-seater stadiums, perimeter fencing was removed, crowd-control procedures were overhauled, and stadium licensing and safety standards were strengthened. Hillsborough consequently became both a symbol of a prolonged struggle for justice and the catalyst for the modernization of football grounds across England.

**Liverpool, England (CNN) —** Chants of “Justice for the 96” rang around Anfield as Andy Burnham addressed the final annual memorial service for those killed in the Hillsborough disaster.

Burnham, a longtime campaigner for the victims’ families and then a senior Labour lawmaker, was met with the chant as thousands gathered at Liverpool’s stadium to remember those who died in the crush during an FA Cup semifinal on April 15, 1989.

The service marked the 27th anniversary of the disaster and came as fresh inquests into the deaths were nearing their conclusion. Burnham praised the families and survivors for their decades-long fight to uncover the truth and secure accountability.

The memorial ended with an emotional rendition of Liverpool’s anthem, “You’ll Never Walk Alone,” sung by those inside the stadium as scarves were raised in tribute.

It was the last large-scale annual Hillsborough memorial held at Anfield, with families saying the approaching conclusion of the inquests made it an appropriate moment to bring the tradition to a close.

Later in April 2016, a jury found that the victims had been unlawfully killed and that the behavior of supporters had not contributed to the disaster.

The death toll was long recorded as 96. It was formally revised to 97 after Andrew Devine, who suffered life-changing injuries at Hillsborough and died in 2021, was ruled to have been unlawfully killed as a result of the disaster.
